name: Cattail (bulrush / reedmace)
habitat: Standing fresh water and its margins — pond edges, ditches, marshes, slow river backwaters. It grows in dense single-species stands.
identify: The brown cigar-shaped seed head on a tall stiff stem is unmistakable and persists through winter.
Long strap-like leaves, 1-3 cm wide, flat, rising from the base with no midrib, arranged in a flattened fan.
Growing in water or saturated ground, in a dense colony.
A clear thick gel sits between the leaf bases at the bottom of the plant.

lookalikes.name: Yellow flag iris
lookalikes.danger: Toxic — the rhizome causes severe gastrointestinal illness, and the sap is a skin irritant. It grows in exactly the same water margins and its young leaves look very like cattail.
lookalikes.tell: Iris leaves have a raised MIDRIB down the centre and are held in a flat fan of overlapping bases; cattail leaves have no midrib and are more rounded across the back. Iris never bears the brown cigar seed head — check for last year's stems in the stand before you dig anything.

lookalikes.name: Sweet flag
lookalikes.danger: Low in passing, but it is not cattail and some strains carry beta-asarone.
lookalikes.tell: Sweet flag has a crimped wavy leaf edge, a distinct midrib, and smells strongly sweet and spicy when crushed. Cattail has no smell.

preparations.method: Peel back the outer leaves at the base of the plant and scrape out the clear gel.
preparations.for_use: A cooling dressing for burns, sunburn, blisters and small wounds; traditionally used as a mild antiseptic and to slow ooze.

preparations.method: Dig the rhizome, wash it, crush it in water, let the starch settle, pour off the water and dry the starch.
preparations.for_use: Carbohydrate — the highest-calorie part of the plant.

preparations.method: Bend the male flower spike into a bag in early summer and shake.

cautions: Cattail concentrates whatever is in its water. It is used deliberately in effluent treatment, so a stand below a farm, a road or an industrial site is holding that runoff in its tissue. Harvest only from clean water.
Positively identify by the seed head, not by the leaf. The iris confusion is the one that hurts people.
The gel is not sterile and is not a substitute for cleaning a wound.
evidence: Extremely well attested as a food plant across the northern hemisphere. The burn and wound use of the gel is traditional; laboratory evidence is limited.
